paras: The attempted lynching of Al Howe and Tom Benway took place at Sun River Crossing, Montana Territory, on the night of August 29, 1881, when four men put ropes around the necks of the two young men to force them to confess to stealing money. Both survived, and four men were bound over to the grand jury on a charge of attempting to hang them. The Benton Weekly Record condemned the affair as an outrage, and a Sun River correspondent of the Rocky Mountain Husbandman mocked it as an "amateur hanging bee."

According to the Benton Record, a sum of $50 had been stolen from a man at the Crossing, and suspicion fell on two young men. The Husbandman's correspondent named the loser as Bill Devine, whose saloon stood at the scene. No report gives the race of the victims or of the men who seized them.

In the Benton Record's account, a mob got the first suspect out of his house on the pretext that he was to attend a trial, put a rope around his neck and a pistol to his head, and ordered him to confess. He protested his innocence, and in the confusion after several shots and cries of murder he threw off the noose and escaped in the dark. The mob then took the second young man from his bed and dragged him about by the rope until he was "half dead," releasing him when he would not confess, his neck swollen, chafed and bleeding.

The Husbandman letter told it differently: Devine, John Gallagher, Jacob Meagher and one Flinn led both men to a telegraph pole in front of Devine's saloon, where one kicked Flinn and got away. The other, "a boy," was strung up three times and each time denied the theft, after which Devine proposed taking him to a tree to hang him "for good." On the way he slipped the rope and escaped while shots were fired after him.

Deputy Sheriff Tom Healy returned to Sun River with Edward Donnelly, arrested on a warrant from Justice J. B. Traxer for his part in the abuse of the two boys. On September 6 Justice Billings bound over Wm. Devine, Ed. Donnelly, Wm. Maher and Wm. Flynn in $1,000 each to await the grand jury on a charge of attempting to hang Howe and Benway. Devine gave bond, and the other three were sent to the Helena jail to await trial. No report of the grand jury's action or of a trial was found in the coverage.

The Benton Weekly Record ran the fullest coverage, beginning with "A Dastardly Outrage" on September 8, which withheld the attackers' names for what it called prudential reasons and called the affair "totally without excuse." A week later it printed the committal telegram under "Four of the Ruffians Committed" and added its hope that the "would-be hangers" would go to prison. The Husbandman's Sun River correspondent, writing on September 4, treated the attack with sarcasm as a confession drawn "in the old reliable vigilantee style" and hoped the four would be "made an example of." Both papers sided with the victims, and neither carried a defense of the attackers.

The date differs: the charge and the Benton Record give Monday, August 29, while the Husbandman letter says the night of "the 27th," at about 2 a.m. The two papers agree on Devine and Flynn but differ on the other two accused, the committal naming Donnelly and Maher where the letter named Gallagher and Meagher. The Benton Record said that everything short of an actual hanging was done, while the Husbandman said the boy was strung up three times. Only the Husbandman letter said that the young man was made deputy sheriff and arrested all four himself, taking them to Dearborn "as there is no justice here."

bases: A mob put ropes around the necks of two young men accused of theft and, by the charge later brought, attempted to hang them; neither was killed (A2, A3, A4).

Four men acting without legal authority under the pretext of punishing a theft (A3, A4; a 'mob' in A2) tried to force a confession with a noose, but both victims survived, so no one was killed (A2, A4).

The Benton Weekly Record (A1, A2, A3) and a Sun River correspondent of the Rocky Mountain Husbandman (A4) independently report a mob with ropes seizing two young men accused of theft at Sun River and the arrest of four men, though they differ on the date, the names of two of the accused and the sequence of events.
